parts.title: The case of the missing cake
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last Saturday, my little cousin Tom and I became detectives. We were staying at our grandmother's house, and just before lunch, a big chocolate cake disappeared from the kitchen table. Grandma was very upset, because she had baked it for a party.

We started by looking for clues. On the floor, there were small brown footprints that led from the kitchen to the garden. "The thief has dirty shoes," Tom said, and wrote it in his notebook. There was also a little cream on the door handle.

We followed the footprints across the grass until they stopped under a big tree. There, we found the empty plate. Next to it was Max, our neighbour's dog, who was fast asleep with chocolate on his nose.

We took the plate back to Grandma, and she could not stop laughing. She said that she would bake another cake and keep it in the fridge. Tom wants to be a real detective now, and he has asked for a magnifying glass for his birthday.

options: A cake she had made was gone
questions.explanation: A big cake disappeared, and she had baked it for a party.

questions.explanation: There were small brown footprints.

options: To a tree in the garden
questions.explanation: They stopped under a big tree.

questions.explanation: Max, the neighbour's dog, was asleep with chocolate on his nose.

parts.title: The queen of crime
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Agatha Christie is one of the most famous writers in the world. [1] Her books have been sold more than two billion times, and only the Bible and Shakespeare have sold more.

She was born in 1890 in the south of England. As a child, she did not go to school. [2] She learned to read when she was only five, and from then on she spent hours with books.

During the First World War, she worked in a hospital. [3] This knowledge later helped her to write about poisons in her stories.

Her first detective book appeared in 1920. [4] It introduced Hercule Poirot, a little Belgian detective with a famous moustache.

She wrote over eighty books in her life. [5] People still enjoy trying to guess who the criminal is before the end.
sentences: He was her favourite character, and she became tired of him.
At the age of ten, she moved to a school in Paris.
There, she learned a great deal about medicines.
No other writer of detective stories has been as successful as she has.
Some of them have been made into films and television series.
It was soon followed by many more cases for him to solve.
Her mother taught her at home, in a house full of books.
She was already well known when she was still quite young.

gaps.explanation: No other writer has been as successful; the next sentence gives sales.
Her mother taught her at home, which explains why she did not go to school.
There, she learned about medicines, which leads to poisons in her stories.
It was followed by many more cases for Poirot, introduced in the sentence before.
Some of them were made into films, and the next sentence says people still enjoy them.

parts.title: A message about a book
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Hi Gaby, Have you finished the detective book that I lent you? I am dying to know [1] you think of it. I read it in two days, and I could not stop turning the pages. The ending was a big surprise, [2] I had guessed that the butler was the criminal. It is the first time that a book has [3] me wrong! If you have not read the last chapter, please do not tell me [4] I have finished it. I [5] already bought the next book in the series, and I will start it tonight. Perhaps we could meet on Saturday and talk about both books. I will bring some biscuits, [6] you can make the tea. Best, Gwen

parts.title: How finger marks solve crimes
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Every person has a different pattern on the ends of their fingers. We call this a finger mark. Even twins do not have exactly [1] same finger marks. Detectives have used them to catch criminals for more than a hundred years. When somebody touches a glass or a door, they leave a tiny mark [2] oil from their skin. Police officers cover the mark with a fine powder, and then it becomes easy to see. They take a photograph of it and compare it [3] the prints of people who have been arrested before. Today, a computer can search millions of finger marks in a few seconds. Of course, a criminal who wears gloves will not leave any marks, [4] it is not always so easy to solve a case. Police also look for other clues, [5] as hair, clothes or blood. Together, all these small pieces of evidence help them to tell the true story of what happened [6] the crime scene.

gaps.explanation: The same finger marks: a fixed phrase.
A mark of oil from their skin.
A criminal who wears gloves leaves no marks, so it is not easy.
Such as hair or clothes: a fixed phrase.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You found the spare key, Gus? I thought it was lost for good.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I looked in my coat pocket first, because that’s where I always put things, but there was only an old ticket. Then I was about to call the locksmith.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: And what happened?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I went to move the cushions, because I dropped my phone there yesterday. When I pushed the sofa, I saw something shining on the floor. It had been there all the time, next to a pen.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: My guess was behind the door, where you keep the hooks.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I checked there as well, twice. Never mind. It’s solved.

question.explanation: The coat pocket only had a ticket and he checked the door twice, but he saw the key shining on the floor when he moved the sofa.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Police are asking for help after a robbery at Baker’s jewellery shop on Mill Street. The owner locked up himself at ten in the evening, and nothing was wrong then. Some neighbours remember a noise at about two in the afternoon of the day before, but that was only a delivery van, so it is not connected. We know that the alarm rang at two o’clock this morning, when the street was empty, and the thieves left in a few minutes. If you were in the area, or if you have a camera on your house, please contact Millbrook police station. Every detail may help us, however small.

question.explanation: The shop was locked at ten and the afternoon noise was a delivery van; the alarm rang at two o’clock this morning.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: How was the new detective film, Gwen? Was it as scary as the posters said?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: The posters promised a lot. It was supposed to be frightening, but I didn’t jump once. It was long, three hours, but I didn’t look at my watch.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So did you enjoy it?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Not very much. After half an hour I knew who did it. The clues were so obvious, the man with the scar, the strange letter. I could guess the end, so there was no surprise.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: My brother said the same.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Next time I’ll choose a comedy.

question.prompt: What did the woman think of the film?
options: It was too easy to guess
question.explanation: It was not scary and the length did not bother her, but she knew who did it after half an hour and could guess the end.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Gray, your bike! Where was it? I thought somebody stole it.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So did I. On Monday I walked round the school, because a girl said that she had seen one like mine, but it was a different make.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: And your garden? You often leave it by the fence.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I looked there a hundred times. Then yesterday I went to buy milk, and there it was, behind the shop, near the bins. Somebody had just left it there.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s lucky!

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I know. It only needed some air in the tyres.

question.prompt: Where did the boy find his bike?
question.explanation: The school bike was a different make and he looked in the garden many times; he found it near the bins behind the shop.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Hi Gus, it’s Gemma. I’m phoning about your notebook, the red one with the maths notes. You asked me whether I had it, and I haven’t, I’m afraid. I thought about borrowing it on Tuesday, but I decided not to, because I have my own notes. Gilda wanted it too, and I think she is going to ask next week for her project, but she hasn’t done it yet. The person who has it is Gabe. He took it on Wednesday, for the exam. I’m sure that he will give it back on Friday, because I see him every day. Call me if you need anything else.

question.explanation: Gemma did not borrow it and Gilda has not asked yet; Gabe took it on Wednesday for the exam.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You tell great mystery stories, Gideon. Where did you get the one about the missing ship?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Not from my uncle, though he talks all day. He mostly tells jokes, and I think he makes up half of them. And my teacher only gives us books to read.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Who then?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Mrs Hartley. She has been our neighbour for fifty years, and she’s ninety-one. I take her some biscuits every Sunday, and she tells me about the town in the war. She remembers everything.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That sounds lovely.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: It is. I always go home with a new story.

question.explanation: The uncle tells jokes and the teacher gives books; Mrs Hartley, who lives next door, tells him stories on Sundays.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Are you coming to Leo’s party on Saturday, Gaby?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I want to, but I’m not sure. I had a cold last week and felt quite ill, but I’m much better now, so that’s not a problem. And I’m not going away until the holidays, in August.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So what’s the problem?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I have to see the dentist at five, and it was the only appointment they had. If it finishes early I’ll come, but it may take a long time.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Come anyway, even if you’re late.

turns.speaker: f

parts.title: Understanding the main idea
parts.instructions: Listen to six short conversations and choose the best answer.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Well, what did you think of the mystery dinner, Gray?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Ninety pounds is a lot, I must say, but the food was lovely, so I didn’t mind.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: The price? My aunt paid, so I can’t complain. But the actors weren’t great. One forgot his words.

turns.speaker: m

question.explanation: He thinks it is expensive and she thinks the actors were poor, but both say that the idea was different from anything else they know.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: It was the gardener, Gwen. I’m sure. His shoes were muddy and he was near the study.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Maybe, but the garden is full of mud after the rain. Everybody’s shoes are muddy.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: He said he was in the kitchen, and the cook says that he wasn’t.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: She also told us she heard nothing, so she isn’t very reliable. I’d wait. You have a story, not proof.

turns.speaker: m

turns.speaker: f

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Still on the crossword, Gideon? You’ve been at it since lunch.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I know. I have four clues left and my head hurts.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Do you want a hint? I did one like this last week.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: No, don’t tell me! I’m not angry, honestly. It’s actually the best part. If you give me the answer, there’s no fun.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I thought you’d be furious by now.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I might be in an hour. But I’ll keep trying. Give me twenty minutes and a coffee.

question.prompt: How does the man feel about the crossword?
options: Angry that it is so hard
question.explanation: He refuses a hint, says it is the best part and asks for twenty more minutes, so he wants to keep trying.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I can’t find my wallet. Everything was in it, even my bus pass.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Where did you last have it?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: In the café, I think. I’ll buy a new one. I need one anyway.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: But your cards and your bus pass! Cancelling them takes ages. Don’t spend any money yet.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Should I call the police then?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It’s too early for that. They would ask if you’d looked everywhere. Walk back the way you came, from the café to the station, step by step, and ask in the shops. I’d bet it’s on a bench.

question.prompt: What does the woman suggest to the man?
question.explanation: She says not to spend money and that it is too early for the police; she tells him to walk back the way he came and ask in the shops.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Gray, look! There’s a note inside this book. "Meet me under the clock at nine." What do you think?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: We should take it to the police. It could be a crime.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It’s probably just a joke. And the police station is closed on Sundays anyway.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Then should we wait until tomorrow? It might be too late.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Let’s ask the librarian first. She knows who borrowed this book last, and she is here until six.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Good idea. That’s faster than anything else.

question.prompt: What do the friends decide to do about the note?
question.explanation: The police station is closed and waiting may be too late, so they go to the librarian, who knows who had the book.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Gus, you look terrible. Did you break something? I heard glass this morning. Was it the kitchen window?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: No, that was the cat. She knocked a glass off the table. It’s not that.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Is it your phone? You lost it last month.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: It’s here in my pocket. The problem is Dad’s message. He told me to be at the station at four, and I only read it at six. He waited for two hours in the cold.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Oh no. Is he angry?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: He says he isn’t, but I feel awful.

question.prompt: What is the boy most upset about?
question.explanation: The glass was broken by the cat and the phone is in his pocket; he is upset because he read his father’s message two hours late.

parts.title: A talk about a famous detective
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: nathalie
turns.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Today I’d like to talk about the most famous detective in fiction, Sherlock Holmes, and about the writer who invented him, Arthur Conan Doyle. Many people think that Doyle was English, because the stories happen in London, and he lived in the south of England for years. But in fact he was born in Edinburgh, so he was a Scottish writer. He was also a doctor, and he started to write while he waited for patients who never came. The first Holmes story appeared in eighteen eighty-seven. Some people believe it was in eighteen ninety-one, but that is when the stories became really popular in a magazine. Now, a few facts about the detective. Holmes lives at 221B Baker Street, and he shares the flat with his friend, Doctor Watson. There is another doctor in one of the stories, Doctor Mortimer, but he only visits once. Watson tells most of the stories, and he is the one who writes everything down. Holmes is very clever, but he has some strange habits. He doesn’t play football, and he doesn’t play the piano, as some films show. When he is thinking, he plays the violin, often at night, which makes Watson rather angry. Doyle wrote four long novels about Holmes and also fifty-six short stories. Together that makes sixty adventures, and readers still enjoy them today. Finally, if you would like to learn more, there is a museum in Baker Street. It is open every day. On Sundays it used to open at ten, but now every day it opens at half past nine, and it closes at six. The tickets are cheaper online, so please look at the website. Thank you for listening.

gaps.prompt: The creator of Holmes was a ___ author
gaps.explanation: Doyle lived in England and the stories are in London, but he was born in Edinburgh, so he was Scottish.

gaps.prompt: The first Holmes story was published in ___
gaps.explanation: The first story appeared in eighteen eighty-seven; eighteen ninety-one is when they became popular.

gaps.prompt: Holmes shares his flat with Doctor ___
gaps.explanation: He lives with Doctor Watson; Doctor Mortimer only visits once.

gaps.prompt: When Holmes thinks, he plays the ___
gaps.explanation: He does not play the piano; when he thinks he plays the violin.

gaps.prompt: Doyle wrote ___ short stories about Holmes
gaps.explanation: He wrote four novels and fifty-six short stories.

gaps.prompt: Every day the museum opens at ___
gaps.explanation: It used to open at ten on Sundays, but now it opens at half past nine every day.

parts.title: An interview with a police detective
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Gideon, is real police work like television?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Not really, I’m afraid. On television, a detective solves everything in one hour, and there is always a chase. Sometimes there is danger, and I have had a few bad evenings, but it’s rare. And most days aren’t exciting at all. I read papers and make phone calls. A real case can take months, and some take years before we find the answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What does a good detective need?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: People imagine that you must be strong and quick, and it helps to be fit, but I have caught more thieves with my head than with my legs. I use a computer every day, like everybody, though the young officers are better than me. What really matters is being patient and remembering details, a name, a face, something that somebody said three weeks ago.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Is there a part of the job that you don’t like?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: The reports are boring, but I write them and forget them. And I don’t mind working at night, because after twenty years I am used to it. The hardest part is talking to the families after a crime. You can’t make anything better, and you see how much they suffer. Even now, I find it difficult to choose the right words.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What does your wife say about your work?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: She jokes a lot. She says I am always at the office, but that isn’t true, because I work normal hours now. What she tells everybody is that I talk in my sleep, saying names and places. Last month I woke up and shouted, "It was the brother!" She laughed for an hour.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you enjoy most?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Medals? We get them sometimes, but mine are in a drawer. I don’t want to see my name in the newspapers either, and my boss prefers it when we keep quiet. What I love is the moment when the pieces fit. For weeks you have a hundred little facts that mean nothing, then one phone call, and suddenly everything is clear.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How do you relax after a hard week?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Some colleagues play football on Fridays, and I joined them once, but I hurt my knee. I thought reading crime books would be nice, but after work it feels like more of the same. So I walk along the river near my house. An hour there, without my phone, and I forget the whole thing.

questions.prompt: How is real police work different from television?
questions.explanation: Danger is rare and most days are not exciting; a real case can take months or years.

questions.prompt: What does a detective need most?
questions.explanation: Being fit helps and he uses a computer, but what matters is being patient and remembering details.

questions.prompt: What does his wife say about him?
